articles.title: History’s lesson for taxing wealth today
articles.text:
Published on
Let's Talk Development

History’s lesson for taxing wealth today

Sacha Dray

Camille Landais

Stefanie Stantcheva

August 25, 2026

This page in:

English

English

What can 19th-century U.S. property tax records tell developing countries about taxing the wealthy today? / Image: Shutterstock

U.S. property tax records spanning more than a century show how governments once measured and taxed wealth at scale—and how gaps between assessed and market values ultimately undermined the system.
Proposals for taxing wealth, reforming estate taxation, and better measurement of billionaire fortunes are back on the policy agenda. Yet these debates rarely draw on historical experiences that show what wealth taxation looked like at scale, how well it measured the assets of the wealthy, or why wealth taxation ultimately retreated. This learning is overdue and matters as much for advanced economies as it does for developing countries, where property taxes remain the most underutilized fiscal tool and both revenue needs and inequality issues are pressing.
In a new paper, we build the first comprehensive, high-frequency annual wealth series spanning more than one hundred years using a largely overlooked source: the records of the General Property Tax in the United States. From 1800 until the Great Depression, this tax aspired to cover all private property, including land, buildings, livestock, financial assets, and, before emancipation, enslaved people. Compiled from thousands of state auditors’ reports and Census Bureau publications, our analysis offers a window into how wealth was measured, taxed, and documented at scale, with lessons applicable today.

When Income Data Fails, Wealth Data Steps In
For context, the General Property Tax generated substantial revenue, averaging 4 percent of GDP over 1850-1940, at a time when wealth accumulation was growing rapidly (fig. 1). Federal income taxation as we know it was only established in 1913, so governments were financing themselves almost entirely through taxing property at the time.
High-frequency property tax records reveal that private wealth grew from roughly three times GDP in 1800 to five times by the eve of World War I, punctuated by a collapse to an all-time low of 195 per cent of GDP at the end of the Civil War. The all-time peak came in 1932, in the depths of the Great Depression: at 580 per cent of GDP, it reflects output collapsing faster than asset values, a reminder that this ratio can rise for bad reasons as well as good. Today, private wealth is again above five times GDP after four decades of asset-price growth close to all time-highs.
Wealth at this scale and volatility is precisely what income-based tax systems are poorly equipped to measure. Today, policymakers concerned about the wealth of the ultra-rich face the same structural problem as back then: tax records only capture income flows and not economic capacity of the richest individuals. Capital gains can go unrealized, business income can be deferred, and much wealth today sits in assets that generate no reportable income from real estate to private equity. As a result, income-based systems understate the economic power of those at the top.
A direct tax on the stock of wealth, assessed periodically at or near market value, sidesteps many of these difficulties. The historical American experience shows that such a system can be administered at scale, even with nineteenth-century institutions and information technology. The challenge, as we describe below, lies in doing it well.

The Central Problem Is Accurately Measuring Wealth
The most important historical lesson from taxing wealth is the gap between assessed and market values. Local assessors, often elected and untrained, valued property well below market price, reducing revenue collected and creating incentives for non-compliance. As a result, the national average assessment (the share of market value captured in assessments) fell from about 83 per cent in 1850 to roughly 40 per cent by the early twentieth century, and far lower in some states.
Under-assessment remains one of the most persistent problems in property taxation today, with well-documented under-valuation of high-value real estate in the US, the UK, and even worse cases in developing countries. Under-valuation can be regressive: if costly properties are assessed at a lower share than cheaper ones, the effective rate on the wealthy is lower.
Recovering market values from administrative data demands investment in independent valuation. The nineteenth-century Census Bureau sent agents into the field, surveyed thousands of experts, and checked assessments against sale prices. Without that infrastructure, the base is whatever assessors say, usually too low for the assets of the wealthy.

Comprehensive Wealth Statistics Are a Public Good
Comprehensive data collection was a precondition for General Property Tax, not a by-product. The decennial Census wealth publications documented property values, exemptions, assessment practices, and legislative change in every state, letting governments track wealth and hold assessors accountable for regional disparities. The parallel to today is direct. The OECD, the EU, and many economists now call for national wealth registers, and several Nordic countries already maintain them. One usual objection is cost. But the cost of not collecting the data is being unable to know how wealth is distributed, how fast it grows, and who pays their fair share. The data also reveals something the tax debate rarely confronts directly: the persistence and growth consequences of wealth concentration.

Wealth Inequality Is Persistent and Hurts Prosperity
Our long-run wealth data shows that spatial inequality across US counties was historically high and never converged: the wealthiest 10 per cent of counties held around 70 per cent of total US property by 1930, and rank-rank correlations between county wealth in 1870 and 1930 stay above 0.6. Places that were wealthy after the Civil War were still overwhelmingly likely to be wealthy sixty years later, with more populous counties both wealthier and faster-growing. This persistence is stronger in wealth than income data, so income convergence can mask stubborn inequality in the stock of assets.
Inequality within places also tracks slower growth. Counties with wealth more concentrated in the top decile in 1870 grew significantly more slowly over the next sixty years, even after controlling for geography, demography, and economic structure. Human capital is a key channel: more unequal places accumulated less education. Replicated across hundreds of counties within one country, this marks wealth concentration as a drag on long-run prosperity.

A Lesson for Developing Countries
These lessons are particularly relevant for developing countries, where property taxes raise only around 0.1 per cent of GDP in emerging Asia and Africa, and with property tax the most under-utilized tax in developing countries. The binding constraint is rarely the tax rate but the same measurement problem the nineteenth-century United States faced, only larger: assessment rolls are incomplete or decades out of date, the assessed-market gap can dwarf anything in our series, and cadastral records may not exist at all. The returns to investing in valuation and wealth statistics are high, and this infrastructure is a precondition for domestic revenue, not a luxury for after countries grow rich.

Takeaways for Policymakers
Nineteenth-century America was no model of sophisticated governance. And yet it still assessed, taxed, and documented private wealth at a scale many modern systems have abandoned. The tax had real flaws: uneven administration, patchy coverage of intangibles, pervasive political pressure. Yet it raised substantial revenue and left an extraordinary record of how wealth changed.
Three messages stand out.
1. Income taxation alone cannot reach the wealthiest; a direct tax on wealth stocks, assessed at market value, is feasible and has real advantages.
2. High-quality wealth assessment matters most and can be achieved: without independent valuation and the statistics behind it, a wealth tax is only as good as local assessors allow.
3. Comprehensive wealth data is a public investment that pays off beyond taxation, helping governments understand inequality, target policy, and hold economic power to account.

Sacha Dray

Economist, Economic Policy Unit for Viet Nam, World Bank & Visiting Research Fellow, London School of Economics

UK public M&A: five questions clients are asking in 2026

Contributor: Cathal Deasy

20 Aug 2026

UK public M&A activity has reached levels not seen since 2018, with overseas investors, corporates and private equity buyers targeting high-quality UK businesses. Explore the key questions behind the surge in deal activity.

Download the 2026 UK public M&A trends report

Key takeaways:

Year-to-date public M&A is at levels not seen since 2018, with many $5bn-plus transactions driving outperformance versus the rest of Europe despite economic and geopolitical uncertainty.
Activity is being driven by both corporate and private equity buyers, as acquirers target high-quality UK-listed businesses with strong market positions, resilient operating models and long-term growth potential.
Overseas interest in UK-listed companies has accelerated significantly, with inbound UK public M&A increasing from $38bn to $77bn year-on-year as international buyers seek access to high-quality assets.
Buyer conviction is reshaping deal tactics, with an increase in unsolicited public takeover approaches and repeated public pressure campaigns ("bear hugs"), creating more competitive and complex M&A situations for boards and shareholders.
As buyers adopt more assertive approaches, preparedness has become a strategic imperative for UK boards. A well-defined view of valuation, shareholder perspectives and available strategic options is essential in today's market

Parsys 2

Double click here to edit Go To Section component

CHAPTERS

1. What’s really driving the strength of UK public M&A?
2. Why are overseas buyers looking at UK corporate targets now?
3. Are M&A tactics becoming more aggressive?
4. Which parts of the UK market are attracting the most attention when it comes to M&A?
5. What does current M&A activity mean for boards and management teams?

Parsys 3

UK public M&A activity is at levels not seen since 2018, with many $5bn-plus transactions driving outperformance versus the rest of Europe. And despite continued geopolitical uncertainty, a shifting macroeconomic backdrop and the impact of inflation and interest rates, boardroom confidence has remained resilient.
Activity is being driven by both corporates and private equity buyers, while overseas acquirers are increasingly recognising the value opportunity presented by high-quality UK-listed businesses.
So, what are clients asking about the UK M&A public market in 2026?

1. What’s really driving the strength of UK public M&A?

The scale of M&A activity reflects demand from across the buyer universe. The UK now accounts for approximately 35%1 of European public M&A activity, with larger transactions in particular driving its outperformance relative to the rest of Europe.
Both corporate and private equity acquirers have been active. UK corporate public M&A volumes are up 75% versus full-year 20252, while sponsor public-to-private volumes are up 97%3.
Buyers are pursuing UK businesses with strong strategic positions, resilient operating models and long-term growth potential. The fact that they are prepared to act despite a more complicated geopolitical and macroeconomic environment speaks to the quality of the assets available in the UK.

2. Why are overseas buyers looking at UK corporate targets now?

International interest has accelerated significantly. Inbound UK public M&A has more than doubled year-on-year, rising from $38bn to $77bn4.

Overseas acquirers are recognising the value opportunity presented by high-quality UK-listed businesses. For strategic acquirers able to take a longer-term view, current market conditions can create opportunities to acquire businesses whose underlying value may not yet be fully reflected in their share prices.
That is attracting more international capital into the UK and contributing to increasingly competitive situations for the strongest assets.

Double click here to edit Flourish Column Chart component

Source: Dealogic (data pulled on 4 August 2026). Notes: Data as of 31 July 2026. Announced UK M&A volumes. Includes announced M&A transactions with a deal value of $100m or greater. 1. Acquiror and target nationality is UK. 2. Target nationality is UK and acquiror nationality is non-UK.

3. Are M&A tactics becoming more aggressive?

There are clear signs that M&A buyer tactics are evolving alongside increased conviction.
Large unsolicited takeover approaches with public pressure campaigns, also known as “bear hug” manoeuvres, have been in favour throughout 2026, with bidders increasingly willing to make very public proposals or return with repeated approaches where a target board has been reluctant to engage.
Public approaches can change the dynamics of a transaction quickly. Making an offer public brings shareholders – and potentially other bidders – into the equation, increasing pressure on boards while creating the potential for greater competitive tension.
For buyers, that puts a premium on getting the approach, valuation and execution strategy right from the outset. For target boards, it makes preparedness increasingly important.

4. Which parts of the UK market are attracting the most attention when it comes to M&A?

Public M&A activity has been particularly pronounced across financial services, industrials and business services, but the broader picture is one of significant demand for UK-listed businesses.
The proportion of UK-listed companies subject to takeover offers is higher than in most other major European markets. That is an important distinction: the strength of UK public M&A is not simply the result of a handful of very large transactions. Interest is broad, across sectors and from different types of buyers.
Boards are evaluating their strategic options against a backdrop of consolidation and heightened shareholder focus on value creation. Buyers are identifying businesses with strategic relevance, established market positions and the potential to create long-term value under new ownership.

Double click here to edit new Flourish Bar chart component

Source: Dealogic (data pulled on 4 August 2026). Notes: Data as of 31 July 2026. Transactions classified according to target sector. Announced UK M&A volumes. Includes announced M&A transactions with a deal value of $100m or greater. 1. Professional Services, as per Dealogic sector classification.

5. What does current M&A activity mean for boards and management teams?

Rising inbound interest, more competitive processes and increasingly assertive buyer tactics are making the operating environment more complex for high-quality UK corporates.
For boards, preparedness means having a current view of valuation and strategic alternatives, understanding the shareholder base and being ready to assess an unsolicited approach, potentially under significant time and public-market pressure.
For prospective buyers, increased competition puts greater emphasis on conviction, financing, tactics and certainty of execution. Identifying an attractive acquisition target is only part of the challenge; being positioned to move decisively can be equally important.

articles.title: Beyond winning and losing: What Beijing wants from the Iran war | Brookings
articles.text:
Commentary

Beyond winning and losing: What Beijing wants from the Iran war

Zhao Long

Zhao Long

Director and Senior Fellow, Institute for International and Security Studies
- Shanghai Institutes for International Studies

August 20, 2026

China does not see the war primarily as a contest over who gains or loses influence. Its more immediate concern is whether the conflict produces consequences that threaten China’s economic interests, strategic environment, or room for maneuver.
Beijing remains concerned about what it sees as the risks of unrestrained American power, including the use of military force and increasingly assertive approaches toward strategic chokepoints, critical resources, and political affairs abroad.
In ending the war and restoring regional order, there may be more room for practical U.S.-China cooperation than either side is currently willing to acknowledge publicly.

10 min read

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

Editor's note:
This is the 17th essay of Assessing China’s “Lost in translation: Decoding Chinese strategic narratives” series. The full collection of essays can be found here.

As the U.S.-Israeli military campaign against Iran enters its sixth month, Washington’s debate about China and the Iran war often begins with a deceptively simple question: Is China winning or losing from the conflict? Some argue that the war is a strategic gift to Beijing, weakening U.S. influence in the Middle East while strengthening China’s position as a diplomatic and economic power. Others contend that because Iran is an important Chinese partner, the weakening of Iran must ultimately weaken China as well.
In practice, China does not see the war primarily as a contest over who gains or loses influence. Its more immediate concern is whether the conflict produces consequences that threaten China’s economic interests, strategic environment, or room for maneuver. Beijing’s approach is therefore less about exploiting the war than about managing its fallout: containing spillover, reducing risks, diversifying dependencies, avoiding strategic entanglement, and finding areas of overlap. The central question is not who wins or loses, but what kind of regional and international order emerges from the conflict—and how much instability China will have to absorb.
Contain the spillover
China has powerful incentives to see the conflict end as quickly as possible. As the world’s largest crude oil importer, China imported roughly 11.6 million barrels per day in 2025 and is highly exposed to disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz. In June 2026, China’s crude imports fell to 7.12 million barrels per day, the lowest level in almost a decade. Yet Beijing has not faced an immediate energy crisis. Inventories, procurement adjustments, and alternative suppliers—including Russia—have given China considerable room to absorb temporary disruptions.
The bigger concern is systemic. Prolonged conflict can destabilize energy prices, disrupt shipping, increase insurance costs, damage regional infrastructure, and generate broader supply-chain shocks. The Strait of Hormuz is part of the infrastructure supporting the global trading system.
For Beijing, therefore, the problem is not simply energy scarcity. It is the possibility that a regional war could spill over into wider disruption of global trade and supply chains. China’s interest in ending the war is fundamentally an interest in stability.
Reduce the risks
There is a widespread assumption in Washington that because China helped facilitate the Saudi-Iranian rapprochement in 2023, Beijing should now be able to “deliver peace” in the Middle East. This greatly overestimates both China’s capabilities and its ambitions.
China is trying to help end the conflict, but it is doing so primarily through diplomatic de-escalation rather than coercive intervention. The reason is straightforward. China does not possess the alliance network, military infrastructure, or regional command structure that the United States has developed over decades. More importantly, Beijing has little interest in assuming responsibility for being the Middle East’s security guarantor.
The regional security landscape is itself changing. On August 7, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan signed a joint defense agreement. Some observers have already compared the arrangement to a potential “Middle Eastern NATO.” The analogy is premature, but it reflects a broader regional desire to diversify security partnerships rather than rely entirely on a single external security provider.
Rather than seeking to fill the security vacuum, China has focused on maintaining communication with Iran, the Gulf states, Pakistan, Arab organizations, and other major powers. In May, Foreign Minister Wang Yi explicitly supported Pakistan’s mediation between Washington and Tehran and encouraged Islamabad to continue its efforts to help resolve the Hormuz issue.
This approach resembles China’s position on the Ukraine war. When a conflict involves major military powers and China is not the cause of the war or a party to it, Beijing generally sees neither a particular responsibility nor a realistic possibility of becoming the primary mediator. When the belligerents still believe that military means can improve their bargaining position, mediation has limited room to operate.
China therefore tends to focus first on preventing escalation, containing spillover, and preserving the possibility of eventual diplomacy. In that sense, China is acting less as a traditional mediator than as a risk-reduction agent.
Diversify the dependencies
One of the clearest lessons Beijing is drawing from the crisis is that resilience requires reducing excessive dependence on any single country, route, or chokepoint. This applies to energy, transportation, trade, and financial connectivity.
The strategic logic behind projects such as the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway, the Trans-Caspian Corridor, and Arctic shipping routes is therefore becoming more important. These are not simply economic projects; they can also provide alternative routes when traditional maritime corridors become vulnerable.
The same logic applies to China-Russia relations. Instability in the Gulf increases the strategic value of Russia as an energy supplier, while disruptions to maritime routes naturally increase the value of land-based energy connections, including the Power of Siberia 2 gas pipeline project. But it would be a mistake to interpret this as the activation of a Sino-Russian alliance.
China’s energy strategy is based on diversification, not dependence. Even when Beijing and Moscow share a strong political interest in expanding energy cooperation, China continues to pay close attention to prices, investment structures, commercial terms, and market conditions. China does not want to replace dependence on the Gulf with dependence on Russia. Its objective is to have fewer dependencies altogether.
Avoid entanglement
In June, Wang explicitly framed the conflict in terms of four lessons. From Beijing’s perspective, the war demonstrates the danger of both initiation and entanglement. When major powers confront security challenges, they should place greater emphasis on restraint rather than allowing power to be used without limits according to the logic of the jungle.
China seeks strategic partnerships that serve its development agenda—not arrangements that automatically draw China into other countries’ confrontations. This helps explain why Chinese strategic thinkers have shown relatively little interest in transforming the comprehensive strategic partnership with Iran into a hard-security alliance. China has neither provided nor intends to provide weapons to either side in an ongoing armed conflict. Beijing views overly expansive definitions of “dual-use items” with skepticism, seeing them as a convenient way to assign blame for setbacks on the battlefield. Before the current conflict, China and Iran did engage in arms sales and military exercises, but these were primarily intended to help Iran maintain a credible defensive capability.
That distinction is particularly important given the broader costs of a protracted war. The economic, security, and geopolitical consequences of an ongoing conflict in the Middle East would extend well beyond the region, with China itself bearing a significant share of the fallout. Beijing therefore has little interest in allowing the conflict to drag on simply to impose costs on the United States. Nor does it want the conflict to reach a point at which China’s own security interests become directly entangled in Iran’s confrontation with Washington.
Find the overlap
Contrary to the assumption that China’s position must necessarily conflict with Washington’s, there is actually more overlap than is often acknowledged.
Beijing’s approach can be summarized through two sets of three principles: On the nuclear issue, China emphasizes non-proliferation, Iran’s right to peaceful nuclear energy under the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, and a negotiated rather than a military solution. On the Strait of Hormuz, China emphasizes freedom and safety of navigation, reopening the waterway through political rather than military means, and addressing the broader security and economic concerns underlying the confrontation.
At the underlying level, these principles are not fundamentally incompatible with U.S. objectives of preventing nuclear proliferation, protecting global commerce, and eventually stabilizing the Gulf.
Hormuz itself illustrates the potential for practical cooperation. Discussions of unilateral control, transit fees, or even military escorts run counter to the strait’s character as a global public good—and are hardly the end state that Beijing, and perhaps Washington as well, would want to see.
The more difficult question is Iran’s economic future. If Washington has genuinely moved away from regime change as an objective, it will eventually have to provide Iran with a credible pathway toward economic survival. Some form of U.S. sanctions relief will be essential, and China is likely to play an important role in Iran’s postwar reconstruction. In other words, in ending the war and restoring regional order, there may be more room for practical U.S.-China cooperation than either side is currently willing to acknowledge publicly.
Of course, this overlap has limits. If Washington continues to seek Iran’s collapse by intensifying its military campaign and broadening the scope of its attacks, thereby further exacerbating the conflict, that would undoubtedly alter Beijing’s current position and strategic calculus.
What comes next?
The postwar Middle East will be more complicated, not less. The conflict has weakened assumptions that Gulf states can simply function as safe havens for capital, talent, energy infrastructure, and global commerce. Even countries that were not direct participants in the fighting have been forced to reconsider the security premium attached to their geographic location.
China’s preferred role is likely to be economic and diplomatic: helping reconnect Iran to regional markets, supporting infrastructure recovery, encouraging political dialogue, and working with other countries to reduce the risks of renewed conflict.
The Iran war, the Red Sea crisis, the Black Sea disruptions, and recurring concerns about the Panama Canal have all reinforced a Chinese perception that key maritime chokepoints should not become instruments of geopolitical coercion. For Beijing, the value of a major maritime corridor ultimately depends on the international community’s ability to preserve it as an open, safe, and predictable artery for global commerce.
Beijing remains concerned about what it sees as the risks of unrestrained American power, including the use of military force and increasingly assertive approaches toward strategic chokepoints, critical resources, and political affairs abroad. But China also recognizes that a complete U.S. retreat could create instability that China itself would have to absorb. China therefore still has an interest in the United States providing regional public goods—provided that U.S. leadership is exercised with greater restraint and does not repeatedly generate new security crises.
China sees a dangerous conflict that has created some strategic opportunities but also substantial economic and security risks. Its priority is to limit those risks, diversify its dependencies, preserve diplomatic options, and avoid becoming entangled in another major power’s war.
Its preferred role is narrower—and perhaps more sustainable: reduce the temperature, keep the channels open, prevent the crisis from spreading, preserve the openness of critical maritime routes, and be ready to help when the parties are finally prepared to make peace.
That may not make China the “winner” of the Iran war. But it may explain more accurately what Beijing believes a responsible major power should do when the costs of instability extend far beyond the battlefield.

Author

Zhao Long

Director and Senior Fellow, Institute for International and Security Studies
- Shanghai Institutes for International Studies

That was from the 2026 Year Ahead last December, and growth so far has been explosive.

At the beginning of the year, there was about $700M worth of tokenized stocks onchain. Today there’s more than $2.7B, which is still small in the grand scheme of things. Traditional markets turn over more than that every few minutes. But the growth is real, and now Robinhood, Coinbase, and Binance have all thrown their hats in the ring.
This issuer race has been a key one to watch. Ondo went from launching last September to almost $1B of stocks today, the biggest in the market, while xStocks now sits at over $700M and has been the fastest grower in recent months. Together, these two now hold roughly 60% of all tokenized stock value.

The top individual tickers by value are also interesting. articles.title: Will An Aging China Save Less?
articles.text:
Will An Aging China Save Less?

Ernan Cui, Yu Wu

Gavekal Dragonomics | 28 Aug 2026

China’s household savings rate has stayed stubbornly high, around 35% of income, for most of the past decade. This stability is surprising as it comes amid rapid demographic changes, with the total population shrinking and the share of the elderly rising. This demographic transformation is only going to accelerate in the coming decade, as a sharp fall in fertility will mean the population becoming even more dominated by the elderly (see The Birth Dearth Deepens). Will this aging of the population finally force a change in China’s high-savings economic model?There are a couple of ways in which demographic changes have been expected to pull down the household savings rate in China. One is through the composition effects of an aging population. Individuals typically build up savings during their working years and spend them down in retirement; as a result, if there are more retired people, the average savings rate should be lower. Another is through generational turnover that changes the dominant pattern of savings behavior. Chinese people whose lives included dramatic shocks, like the Cultural Revolution and the dismantling of the planned economy, are generally thought to be more cautious and risk-averse than the younger generations who have grown up in a more prosperous and stable China. As these newer generations become the largest part of the workforce, they could also pull down the overall savings rate.

articles.title: Girls outperform boys in school. Then the gap reverses. The HCI+ explains why
articles.text:
Published on
Data Blog

Girls outperform boys in school. Then the gap reverses. The HCI+ explains why

Brian Stacy

Nandita Roy

August 27, 2026

This page in:

English

English

Girls often outperform boys in education, but lower employment and fewer years of work experience can reverse that advantage over a lifetime, according to HCI+ data. Pictured, schoolgirls are seen attending a class in West Bengal, India. / Image: Shutterstock

Girls now outperform boys in school in much of the world. Yet men end up with a 21 percent advantage in expected earnings globally. The reason is almost entirely about what happens after school, not during it.
The Human Capital Index Plus (HCI+) measures human capital through working life, to age 65. Its latest update adds three new features that make the data more actionable than ever: a female employment deep dive that pinpoints exactly where women fall behind in the labor market, a NEET deep dive tracking the millions of young people — disproportionately women — who are neither working nor in school between the ages of 18 and 25 and a revamped simulation tool.
Here is what they reveal.

1. The gender gap in human capital is a jobs gap, not a school gap
Women score about 5 HCI+ points higher than men on health and education combined. Yet their total HCI+ score is 19 points lower. Employment accounts for essentially all of it. In South Asia, on-the-job learning alone explains 98 percent of the gender gap. More broadly, the pattern is widespread: in 101 of 145 countries with sex-disaggregated data, women outperform men on health and education but men have higher overall HCI+ scores once employment and work experience are taken into account.
The logic is straightforward. A worker with 30 years of experience in a wage job is roughly two and a half times as productive as someone just starting out, a gain roughly equivalent to completing 12 years of average quality schooling. Work is not only where human capital is put to use; it is where it continues to grow. But because women are less likely to participate in the labor force and often spend fewer years in paid employment, they miss out on years of learning, skill development, and productivity gains that work provides.
Figure 1. Decomposition of the HCI+ gender gap by component

The new female employment deep dive in the HCI+ App shows, country by country, which barrier matters most: whether women are outside the labor force entirely, unemployed, or in jobs where little learning takes place. That distinction drives very different policy responses.

2. Three in ten young people are neither studying nor working
The HCI+ treats the seven years between ages 18 and 25 as a critical window: a young person is either studying, working, or neither. The third group, young people not in employment, education, or training (NEETs), pays a penalty. First, they lose out on the opportunity to accumulate skills during this period. In addition, skills can depreciate over time, so that each year outside work or school reduces skills at an estimated rate of 1.25 percent.
The scale is large. Across 151 countries, roughly one in four young people is a NEET. In low- and middle-income countries, the share rises to one in three. In the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, it hits 41 percent.
Figure 2. Share of youth aged 20 to 24 neither working nor in school, by region, split by sex

The gap is also heavily gendered. Globally, 40 percent of young women aged 20–24 are neither working nor studying, compared to 17 percent of young men. In the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, the figures are 63 versus 20 percent. In South Asia, 55 versus 15 percent.
High NEET rates among young women and lower female employment rates later in life both reduce opportunities to build human capital through work. Together, these patterns help explain why women often outperform men in education yet still accumulate less human capital over their lifetimes. The HCI+ captures both effects: the years of learning and earnings potential lost during the school-to-work transition and the slower accumulation of experience and skills that comes from lower employment in adulthood.
The new NEET deep dive in the HCI+ App examines how post-school pathways differ by country and what that means for human capital accumulation.

3. A revamped simulation tool: From diagnosis to action in a few clicks
Knowing where the gap is large is only useful if you can ask what to do about it. The HCI+ App's simulation tool has been revamped to make that question answerable.

The new simulation lets users isolate any single driver — health, education, or employment — and see its projected effect on future earnings and productivity. It tells you what moves the score, and by how much. A policymaker can now ask: what happens to our economy if we bring more young women into wage employment? Or reduce our NEET rate by ten percentage points? The app gives a data-grounded answer, country by country.
Together with the two new deep dives, the simulation tool reflects what the HCI+ is ultimately for: not just measuring where human capital is being lost but giving governments the tools to do something about it.

articles.title: Protecting our Clients Against Potentially Fraudulent Activity
articles.text:
Protecting our Clients Against Potentially Fraudulent Activity

Protecting Our Clients Against Potentially Fraudulent Activity
Across the industry, we are seeing an increase in bad actors impersonating and misusing corporate brands to get access to personal information and funds from unsuspecting individuals. These activities may involve individuals acting as company representatives and may include fake websites, social media inquiries, or communications that closely resemble official channels.
Please read the below for important reminders that can help protect you from potentially fraudulent activity.
We strongly caution against providing personal data or transferring funds in response to unsolicited requests. For your safety, always verify the authenticity of communications claiming to be from Lazard by contacting us through our official website or known contact points.
Specifically, Lazard will never engage in the following activities:

Sending unsolicited investment proposals or requests for personal information from nonverified persons.
Requesting payments to bank accounts in the names of individuals, third parties, unknown company names, or through payment intermediaries.
Offering unrealistically attractive returns that seem too good to be true.
Expressing urgency to complete an investment or make a payment.
Requesting additional payments to release investments that have already been made.
Requesting money to be sent via social media messaging apps and/or platforms.

If you believe that you have fallen victim to fraud, please contact your bank immediately. Additionally, you should report the incident to law enforcement in your jurisdiction as soon as possible.
The safety and protection of data and information is a priority for Lazard, and we appreciate your careful attention and diligence.
***
Lazard cannot accept any responsibility for any loss, damage, or claims arising from fraudulent activities. Please fully read account disclosures and related policies.

US Treasury demand is holding, but the buyer base is shifting

Treasury demand is evolving, with a notable shift towards more price-sensitive buyers amid changing market dynamics. While Treasury yields are expected to remain elevated in the near term, a gradual decline is anticipated as inflation pressures ease.

The Federal Reserve is likely to maintain a hawkish stance through 2026 due to persistent inflation, but easing services inflation and a cooling labour market may prevent further rate hikes. Long-end yields are projected to fall slowly, influenced by heavy Treasury supply and geopolitical uncertainties, alongside record corporate borrowing linked to AI investments.

Recent data indicates that foreign demand for Treasuries has weakened, leading to increased reliance on domestic investment funds and leveraged investors. The Treasury plans to adjust its issuance strategy, focusing more on shorter-term securities to manage rising borrowing needs effectively.

articles.title: Committing $50M to USHP: The Product Bringing U.S. Home Prices Onchain
articles.text:
Insights / Perspectives / Committing $50M to USHP: The Product Bringing U.S. Home Prices Onchain

Written by:

The Galaxy Team
Galaxy

perspectives • August 10, 2026

Committing $50M to USHP: The Product Bringing U.S. Home Prices Onchain

Worth roughly $55 trillion and comparable in size to the entire S&P 500, U.S. residential housing is one of the world’s largest asset classes. Yet unlike equities, Treasuries, or gold, investors have lacked a simple, liquid way to hold index-level exposure to U.S. home prices. Benchmarks such as the FHFA House Price Index and the Case-Shiller Index exist, but the benchmarks themselves are not investable products. The usual alternatives – homebuilder stocks and public or private REITs – bury home price exposure under operating leverage, management decisions, and equity-market beta. As a result, the largest store of household wealth in America has remained one of the hardest asset classes to own.Galaxy is excited to announce our $50M commitment to USHP, the first digital asset referencing a U.S. home price index, through USHP Limited’s pre-launch institutional round.
The Onchain Efficient FrontierOur thesis at Galaxy is that capital markets are moving onchain, and that an Onchain Efficient Frontier is forming across the full spectrum of risk and return profiles. To date, that frontier has been built largely on crypto-native sources of yield: basis trades, rehypothecation, leverage, and token incentives. Meanwhile, roughly $300 billion of stablecoin supply sits idle, generating little or no yield while quietly losing ground to inflation. We believe the next chapter of onchain asset management will connect that capital to real-world assets with durable, exogenous yield. The strongest candidates are large, historically difficult-to-access asset classes, backed by genuine economic activity rather than reflexive incentives. Few asset classes fit that description better than U.S. housing.U.S. housing is one of the deepest, most stable sources of long-term returns in global markets, yet it has remained largely inaccessible as a simple, liquid index investment. USHP is designed to change that.
A New Way to Access the World's Largest Asset ClassFor generations, U.S. real estate has been one of the most dependable engines of household wealth, and also one of the least accessible. Investing has traditionally required a substantial down payment, a mortgage, local market expertise, and the ongoing responsibilities of property ownership. USHP changes that. It will launch on Ethereum and provide eligible participants liquid, indexed exposure to U.S. home prices without the burdens of owning or managing physical property.We believe the asset class’s historically low volatility, relatively low correlation with other financial assets, and its backing by dollar-denominated real assets will appeal to a range of eligible (non-U.S.) investors. Beyond traditional real estate investors, we believe crypto-native institutions that hold stablecoins, tokenized Treasuries, and other cryptoassets may also value the combination of yield and index-linked exposure that USHP is designed to provide.Over time, we expect that the blockchain and tokenization infrastructure underpinning USHP will be used to support an entirely new category of investment products designed for U.S. homebuyers, creating new ways for households to access, manage, and participate in the economics of residential real estate.
Why We Are InvestingAt Galaxy, we invest in companies that are working to build the financial infrastructure of the future. Throughout the history of capital markets, some of the most impactful innovations have made large, valuable asset classes easier to access, own, and trade. We believe tokenization will do the same for many of the world's largest markets, and U.S. residential real estate is among the most compelling opportunities.Our experience backing companies such as Ethena and Ornn has reinforced our belief that when novel financial products solve a real market need and are designed to scale, adoption can accelerate quickly. We believe USHP has the potential to become another important building block in the onchain economy.We are thrilled to partner with the founding team of the platform that powers USHP. They pair deep crypto-native investing and operating experience with Blackstone Real Estate pedigree and a track record scaling a cutting-edge institutional real estate investment platform. That combination is a pairing we don’t see often.Index Industries is a portfolio company of Galaxy Ventures. Galaxy and its affiliates hold equity in Index Industries, are participating in the pre-launch round for USHP, and expect to serve as an institutional minter of and liquidity provider for USHP, for which they may receive compensation. This post is not an offer to sell, or a solicitation of an offer to buy, any security and is not investment advice. USHP is issued by USHP Limited, a British Virgin Islands company and a subsidiary of the USHP Foundation, and is not available in the United States or to U.S. persons; any offering of USHP will be made only to eligible non-U.S. institutional investors pursuant to the issuer’s offering documents. articles.title: KPMG Receives IDC 2026 Customer Satisfaction Award for Security and Trust Services
articles.text:
KPMG is proud to announce that we have received the IDC 2026 Customer Satisfaction (CSAT) Award for Security and Trust Services. This recognition is based on direct client feedback gathered through IDC's Services Path Survey and we believe it reflects KPMG member firms continued commitment to helping organizations address increasingly complex cybersecurity, trust, and resilience challenges while delivering exceptional client experiences.

Read the report here

opens in a new tab

What the award means

The IDC Services CSAT Awards recognize leading service providers across key services markets based on customer satisfaction ratings collected through IDC's Services Path Survey. As part of the 2026 assessment, KPMG member firms were placed in the highest scoring group among providers of Security and Trust Services and received IDC's 2026 Customer Satisfaction Award for Security and Trust Services.The survey captures feedback from organizations worldwide and evaluates service providers across more than 30 customer satisfaction metrics, providing a broad-ranging view of client perceptions and experiences.

We are honored to receive IDC's 2026 Customer Satisfaction Award for Security and Trust Services. We believe this recognition reflects the trust our clients place in us, the dedication of our professionals, and our commitment to helping organizations navigate today's rapidly evolving cybersecurity and technology landscape while driving meaningful business outcomes.

Laurent Gobbi

Global Cybersecurity and Tech Risk CoE Leader

KPMG in France

Key findings from IDC's research

Client-centric approach KPMG's high customer satisfaction scores reflect our dedication to understanding and addressing the unique needs of each client.Increasing investment in security and trust The Award Report and Findings notes that "87% of companies stated they expect their spending to increase, and 13% expect it to stay the same. No companies reported that they expect a decline in spending, highlighting companies’ strong focus and continued momentum surrounding security and trust services.

The IDC Services Path Survey captures customers' perspectives on the service providers they work with across a broad range of satisfaction measures. KPMG's recognition with IDC's 2026 Customer Satisfaction Award for Security and Trust Services reflects strong feedback from surveyed clients and demonstrates the value organizations place on providers that help them strengthen security, build trust, and navigate an increasingly complex business environment.

Craig Robinson

Research VP, Security and Trust

IDC

KPMG's strengths

The award highlights KPMG’s strengths in trusted brand, experience in business processes, expertise in advanced AI (generative and agentic capabilities), change management, ability to develop tailored IP/solutions, provides effective advisory and consultative services and provides effective management/monitoring (24x7) services.

Why choose KPMG for security and trust services?

At KPMG, we help organizations build confidence in an increasingly complex digital environment through integrated security, privacy, risk, and resilience services.
Working with clients around the world, KPMG member firms can help organizations:Strengthen cyber resilience and reduce security risk.Enhance trust across digital ecosystems and critical business processes.Modernize security capabilities through advanced technologies and AI-enabled solutions.Navigate evolving regulatory and compliance requirements.Build security programs aligned to business objectives and growth strategies.Improve preparedness, response, and recovery capabilities in the face of emerging threats.Our focus is not only on protecting organizations from risk, but also on helping them build and maintain trust with customers, stakeholders, regulators, and employees.

Beyond customer satisfaction: Recognized market leadership

We believe our IDC 2026 Customer Satisfaction Award for Security and Trust Services is complemented by additional recognition from IDC's independent research. KPMG firms were also recognized as a Leader in the IDC MarketScape: Worldwide Cybersecurity Governance, Risk and Compliance Consulting Services 2025-2026 Vendor Assessment, a Leader in the IDC MarketScape: Worldwide Enterprise Governance, Risk and Compliance Services 2025-2026 Vendor Assessment and a Leader in the IDC MarketScape: European Cyber GRC Services 2026 Vendor AssessmentTogether, we believe these recognitions demonstrate both the strength of KPMG firms' Security and Trust Services capabilities and our commitment to delivering exceptional client experiences. While the IDC MarketScape evaluations assess providers' capabilities and strategies, the IDC Customer Satisfaction Award reflects direct client feedback, providing complementary perspectives on the value KPMG professionals deliver to organizations navigating increasingly complex risk, cybersecurity, and trust challenges.Source: IDC 2026 Security and Trust Services CSAT Award (Doc #US46933620e-KPMG, March 2026)

articles.title: On the move: Renovation over relocation?
articles.text:
Joe Wadford

August 2026

Americans are moving less, and the slowdown is broad-based, according to Bank of America account data. Mobility continued to decline in Q2 2026 across income groups, generations and move types, with lower-income households and Millennials seeing the sharpest pullbacks.
Bank of America account data also tells us that while longer-distance relocations have fallen more sharply overall, moves within the same city slowed at a faster rate in Q2 2026. This suggests to us that the resilience of same-city moving deteriorated somewhat in the past quarter. When people do change locales, they still favor smaller cities, especially those in the Midwest.
Moving-related spending is gravitating toward services and online spending, according to Bank of America card data. However, some homeowners are choosing renovation over relocation. Supported by home equity lines of credit (HELOC) loans, this renovation activity may broaden spending growth across home improvement retailers.

Read our full analysis for a more in-depth look at these trends.

Es kann keine Zusicherung gegeben werden, dass Prognosen oder Ziele erreicht werden können. Prognosen basieren auf Annahmen, Schätzungen, Meinungen und hypothetischen Modellen, die sich als falsch erweisen können. Die Wertentwicklung in der Vergangenheit ist kein Hinweis auf zukünftige Renditen. Die Wertentwicklung bezieht sich auf einen Nominalwert, der auf Kursgewinnen/-verlusten beruht und die Inflation nicht berücksichtigt. Die Inflation wirkt sich negativ auf die Kaufkraft dieses nominalen Geldwerts aus. Je nach aktuellem Inflationsniveau kann dies zu einem realen Wertverlust führen, selbst wenn die nominale Wertentwicklung der Anlage positiv ist. Investitionen sind mit Risiken verbunden. Der Wert einer Anlage kann sowohl fallen als auch steigen, und Sie erhalten möglicherweise zu keinem Zeitpunkt den ursprünglich investierten Betrag zurück. Ihr Kapital kann gefährdet sein.

articles.title: Horizons Live: Electric shock
articles.text:
Webinar

Horizons Live: Electric shock
This month’s Horizons report looks at what could happen if electric vehicle adoption moves faster than Wood Mackenzie’s base case. Join us for Horizons Live as our expert panel examines the forces that could drive a faster transition and what it would mean for oil demand, critical minerals and power markets.

Date
2 September 2026

Time
4-5pm BST / 11-12am EST

Wood Mackenzie’s base case sees electric vehicles increasing from 4% of the global passenger and commercial vehicle fleet in 2025 to 25% by 2040. But a combination of higher oil prices, faster progress in Chinese electric vehicle technology and supportive government policy could push adoption significantly further.
In the report’s “electric shock” scenario, global oil demand falls to 99 million barrels per day by 2040, around 5 million barrels per day below the base case. Faster electric vehicle adoption would also put greater pressure on critical mineral supply and electricity networks, while changing the economics of oil refining. Around 40 refineries could close as a result of weaker demand.
This Horizons Live session will bring together Wood Mackenzie’s electric vehicle and energy transition experts to look at what would need to happen for this scenario to play out, where the biggest uncertainties lie and what businesses and investors should be watching.
Join us live as our panel explores how quickly electric vehicles could change the global vehicle fleet, and what a faster transition could mean for oil markets, critical minerals, power systems and energy investment through 2040.

In this webinar, you can expect to learn about:

What could accelerate EV adoption: how oil prices, government policy and advances in electric vehicle and battery technology could push adoption beyond Wood Mackenzie’s base case
China’s role in the transition: why China’s electric vehicle industry could be a major driver of lower costs and higher exports, particularly across emerging markets
What faster EV adoption means for oil: how a potential 5 million barrels per day reduction in oil demand could affect crude markets and refinery economics, particularly in OECD markets
Critical minerals and supply: why copper could be the biggest supply constraint in a faster EV transition, and where additional investment would be needed to meet demand
Pressure on power grids: how rising electricity demand from electric vehicles could affect power systems, and why managed charging will become increasingly important
What to watch: which developments in oil markets, Chinese EV exports, battery manufacturing and government policy could indicate that the faster adoption scenario is starting to take shape

articles.title: View from the markets: Bonds, panic…and crisis? - BNP Paribas Asset Management - United States
articles.text:
By Chris Iggo, Chair of the Investment Institute and CIO for AXA IM Core, BNP Paribas Asset Management

A 6% yield on 30-year US Treasury bonds has not been seen since the end of the last century. Some bond bears think we might see that yield again soon.

A key difference between now and then is that today there is a lot more government debt. Consequently, higher yields threaten a potential bond crisis for governments. That, in turn, might impact on credit and equity markets. Investors need to be more vigilant than ever.

Key macro themes – Threats to economic resilience remain

Key market themes – Potential for volatility to increase post-summer

Bond panic

The bond panic is not likely to turn into bond euphoria. Potential bond rally triggers include weaker economic data, more dovish central banks, or an equity market correction – one which is significant enough to negatively affect the economic outlook. But right now, none of these are present.

Instead, government debt concerns have risen to near-hysterical levels. It is clear why. Debt is a liability for governments, and it is rising. There was a lot of noise around the US Federal debt level exceeding $40 trillion recently.

The bigger the liability gets, relative to income (GDP), then the odds are that there will be higher borrowing costs and potential refinancing difficulties. Such outcomes have negative financial, political, and social implications.

Current concerns about the rise in US government long-term bond yields have pushed the US government into increasing its buy-back operation of long-term Treasury bonds. There has even been talk of using the Treasury’s General Account to fund these buybacks.

Floating unconventional policy ideas is not good for market sentiment. It makes investors question what the motivation is. Given the US is just over two months away from its midterm elections, some may conclude the key motivation is political.

I mentioned recently that rising mortgage rates are not an ideal backdrop for the incumbent government. US 30-year average mortgage rates hit 6.8% recently. There is a hint of panic in the air.

Roughly 22% of outstanding US Treasuries are trading with a market yield above 5%. Those bonds, collectively, were issued with an aggregate average coupon of 3.25%. As a thought exercise, if all the bonds currently yielding more than 5% were to be refinanced today, that would increase the US Treasury’s interest bill by over $4 billion.

Negative trend

Of course, there are complex reasons why long-term yields have been rising. One is the ever-present concern about increasing government budget deficits across the developed world.

The ongoing situation in the Middle East could push inflation higher again, leading to central banks having to tighten monetary policy. There is also an element of normalisation: bond yields were generally higher before the global financial crisis, when they reflected greater levels of nominal GDP growth (largely because inflation tended to be higher).

There has also been an increase in capital demand. This year is on track to be a record year for corporate bond issuance, driven by technology companies raising funds to finance the artificial intelligence infrastructure build.

Net equity issuance should also be positive – again technology companies are at the forefront of this but the recently announced planned IPO by fashion company Shein in Hong Kong ($1.8 billion according to Bloomberg) suggests the demand for capital goes beyond the AI race. Investors are being asked to commit a lot of money.

Increased demand for capital should raise the price of that capital (yields). It certainly seems to have – 30-year government bond yields are up anywhere between 25 basis points in Germany, to 70bps in Japan.

Assets as well

The focus on bonds as a liability is the core of the credit market, and investors need to consider the macroeconomic and credit risks before investing. However, bonds are an asset as well, and an important one for financial institutions and households.

One borrowers’ debt security is another investors’ financial asset. The interest paid by the borrower on the debt represents investment income to the lender.

I will repeat that long-term bonds have not been a great asset in recent years, with bond prices collapsing during the interest rate reset and remaining sensitive to inflation, interest rates, and fiscal developments.

Rising yields based on increased borrowing are ‘dilutive’ – the borrower must pay back more creditors and new borrowing is priced at the higher yield, which means diminished prices for bonds that were issued at lower yields.

With an income focus, bonds are attractive

But looking through the ‘bonds as an asset’ prism, yields are more attractive. Market commentary suggests a 5% yield on 10-year US Treasuries (4.7% currently) would trigger a buying spree. Existing yields in the UK and eurozone are well above current inflation rates and the 10-to-15-year sector looks particularly interesting given the shape of yield curves.

Note that bonds’ income streams are a valuable component of any portfolio. Fixed income strategies that have limited interest rate risk (short duration) and reasonable credit spreads are amongst the most attractive.

Investing in a US five-year corporate bond with a 5.25% coupon today should potentially generate a compound total return of 29% over the maturity of the bond, with the principal repaid as well.

High yield markets offer even greater return potential, albeit with more risk to capital because of the potential for borrowers defaulting (which has been low in recent years).

But long-end volatility might remain, and spread

Income is one thing, but volatility can impact the mark-to-market valuation of a bond portfolio significantly. The US is where risk is most evident, given the uncertainty over the Federal Reserve’s policy direction under new Chair Kevin Warsh, and the fiscal outlook.

Most corporate borrowing is taking place in the US. And keep in mind that US market yields are, to a significant extent, dependent on the willingness of the rest of the world to buy the dollar and US financial assets.

There is no compelling evidence that this is changing, but the more fractious international political environment could impact on flows eventually.

The upside for US yields may be greater than elsewhere as America needs to keep on attracting the most capital. Elsewhere, there are attractive yields in European government and credit markets with less fundamental risk.

In the UK, the gilt market has been volatile and there are concerns about inflation and government borrowing. A significant gilt rally, and therefore lower yields across the sterling market, is unlikely to occur until the next budget – the first under new Prime Minister Andy Burnham – is delivered.

Seatbelts on

The September-to-October period has been one of the more volatile parts of the year historically. The US midterm elections will be a key market focus, as will be the Middle East and energy market developments. If the bond vigilantes get upset, the risk is this will start to push credit spreads wider and impact equity market valuations.

Markets might be due a correction. The sense of us being in a Goldilocks economy is a fragile one. Higher inflation and interest rates are risks. Less optimism about AI is another. The geopolitical backdrop is tense. Bonds might lead the way – they are doing so already. But bonds may also signal the next buying opportunity. A 6% US 30-year yield has not been seen since before the millennium, and one today would make bonds extremely cheap relative to equities.

Performance data/data sources: LSEG Workspace DataStream, ICE Data Services, Bloomberg, BNP Paribas AM, as of 26 August 2026, unless otherwise stated). Past performance should not be seen as a guide to future returns.

articles.title: Tracking federal expenditures in real time | Brookings
articles.text:
Research

Tracking federal expenditures in real time

August 26, 2026

6 min read

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

This tool will update daily shortly after 4 p.m. ET on weekdays, excluding federal holidays, for daily data from the Daily Treasury Statements. Weekend and holiday transactions accumulate to the next business day. Weekly data (totaled from the daily data) will update once the previous full week’s data are complete. Monthly data are updated once a month, shortly after the Monthly Treasury Statements are released on the eighth business day. Totals are the sum of outlay categories, excluding Public Debt Cash Redemptions.

On mobile devices, the tracker is best viewed in landscape.

The Trump administration’s conduct and statements with regard to spending freezes and impoundment, including the Department of Government Efficiency’s (DOGE) activities, have created uncertainty as to whether or not funding is flowing through Treasury’s Bureau of the Fiscal Service to particular programs, agencies, and departments in accordance with the law.
This data tool allows users to track the flow of federal funds in real time. It shows actual daily, weekly, monthly, and annual processed outlays to key programs and departments, as well as to states, Congress, and the Judiciary. This tool only reports outlays of federal funds, meaning the actual transmission of funds from the federal government to another entity.
This tool makes few to no adjustments to the data, meaning that cyclical, seasonal, idiosyncratic, and expected variation in patterns of outlays over time remain. Because this tool only reports outlays, one cannot discern directly whether there is a gap between obligated funds and their outlay. Furthermore, if federal agencies have changed the rate at which they are newly obligating funds (e.g., by declining to sign new contracts), those changes would only gradually be reflected in outlays. Some outlay recipients’ labels and abbreviations are adjusted for clarity and to reflect federal changes to category groupings or labeling conventions.
These data are downloadable and can be used for secondary analysis.

https://www.npr.org/2025/02/14/1231335530/treasury-payments-doge

Listen:

Hear about this tool and potential use cases on NPR's Planet Money

Step one: Select “Compare by year,” or “Outlays over time”
“Compare by year” tab
With the “Compare by year” tab, you can select one outlay recipient at a time to observe how year-to-date outlays (either as a time series or cumulative) compare to patterns in prior years. While the tool defaults to comparing 2026 to 2025 and 2024, users can change which years are shown using the “Select years:” box. Note that, in the cumulative data, we exclude years that do not have data starting in January as well as outlay recipients with no 2026 data.
The below examples from the “Compare outlays by year” tab show daily outlays to the United States Department of Agriculture Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) by “Time series” (above) and “Cumulative year-to-date” (below).

“Outlays over time” tab
With the “Outlays over time” tabs, you can select your desired time period, outlay frequency, and outlay recipients. In these tabs, you can compare up to nine outlay recipients using the “Select outlay recipients” box.
Using daily data, you can select three months, one year, or three years for the time period, and daily, weekly, or a seven-day simple moving average for the outlay frequency. The below example from the “Outlays over time” tab shows daily outlays to SNAP and the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) program in the past year.

Using monthly data, you can select one year or three years for the time period. The below example shows monthly outlays to SNAP (3.6.4), TANF (8.1.11), and Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC) (3.6.3) over the past year.

Step two: Select data from Daily or Monthly Treasury Statement
This interactive allows you to explore date from both Daily and Monthly Treasury Statements. Daily Treasury Statements have high frequency data for a more limited set of outlay recipients. Monthly Treasury Statements have lower frequency data for an extensive set of outlay recipients.

Step three: Select outlay recipient(s)
Once a tab is selected, one can select or search for outlay recipients using the “Select outlay recipient(s)” bar.
To use the “Compare by year” tool, select one outlay recipient at a time. Not every outlay recipient is present for the entire time series. If a particular outlay recipient is not present in 2026, then the “Compare by year” tab will not populate. To use the “Outlays over time” tool, select up to nine recipients by searching for an outlay recipient or by using the dropdown menu. Recipients can include programs like the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program [SNAP], agencies like the National Institutes of Health [NIH], and other recipients of federal funding.
Labels for the outlay recipients in this tool have been edited for clarity and consistency over time and may not directly match those found on the Daily or Monthly Treasury Statements. For daily outlays, we have added common abbreviations to help navigate the tool and made outlay recipient names consistent over time. The glossary lists the names of the outlay line items available in the tool, as reported in the Daily Treasury Statement, as shown in this tool and in full.
For monthly outlays, we have made very few changes to outlay recipient names and have not yet added common abbreviations to aid search. To help navigate the monthly outlays, recipients are labeled with numerical prefixes that reflect the nested structure of programs and are consistent over time. Top-level categories (for example, the Legislative Branch or the Department of Commerce) are designated with a single number (1–32), and each nested subcategory is designated with a decimal. For example, one top level category is “10 Department of Housing and Urban Development.” The first nested categories under housing programs include “10.1 Community Planning and Development,” “10.2 Government National Mortgage Association,” “10.3 Housing Programs,” and several others. To go another level down, under “10.1 Community Planning and Development,” you can find “10.1.1 Community Development Fund,” “10.1.2 Home Investment Partnership Program,” and several others. Totals for each category are calculated from each of its subcategories.

This tool was developed by Lauren Bauer, Noadia Steinmetz-Silber, Riki Matsumoto, and Eileen Powell. It is a work in progress; please contact Lauren Bauer (info@hamiltonproject.org) if you have questions or suggestions. For more information about the tool and its potential uses, listen to the Planet Money from NPR episode “The Big Government Money Pipe Freeze.”
Note that, as of May 2025, you can view outlays by year (time series and cumulative year-to-date) using data from the Monthly Treasury Statements.
